newsitem.title: FINLAND: Usinor chairman confident in 1997 recovery.
newsitem.headline: Usinor chairman confident in 1997 recovery.

text.p: Real demand for steel will rise next year, maybe to the level of 1995, helping prices rise and lifting steel producers' earnings, Francis Mer, chairman of Europe's largest steelmaker Usinor Sacilor, said on Tuesday.

Speaking to a Reuters reporter at the second day of the annual congress of the International Iron and Steel Institute (IISI) here, he said volumes were already improving and that he was "reasonably confident in the overall situation in 1997".

"From a quantitative point of view, things are improving now but from a pricing point of view ... it is clear that results of corporations on a quarterly basis during the last quarter will be on average lower than in the preceding quarters," he said.

"As far as volumes are concerned, it is clear that the last quarter of this year will be improved vis--vis the equivalent quarter of last year because last year we went in a strong reduction of output to reduce inventories," he noted.
Usinor last week announced first half profits falling 65 percent to 833 million francs and said the second half would be weaker. The first half of 1997 would show an improvement, it said.
Some prices already showed signs of a rise, Mer said.
"There are positive signs that during the fourth quarter, some prices will be higher than in the third quarter," he said, adding this was a global trend.
Stainless steel prices for instance are recovering worldwide, he said.
"But Europe presently has quite low prices, so (the recovery) will be probably more significant than in other countries," he added.

"Underlying real demand in Europe has probably slightly decreased in Europe in 96 versus 95 because the economic climate is not very good, we think, we hope that with regard to various forecasts, 1997 will be slightly better," he said.
"I'm not saying that we are facing an economic boom in Europe but everybody agrees that there is good chance for slight improvement in 1997," he said.

The IISI forecast European apparent steel consumption to rise 4.9 percent next year after an expected 7.1 percent slump this year and global growth at 3.4 percent next year would take steel consumption to a record 680 million tonnes.

"... Real consumption in 1997 will be probably slightly higher than in 1996 and maybe at the level of 95, so if you have suppressed the inventory problem, this explains why we are reasonably confident vis--vis an improvement of our overall situation in 1997," Mer said.
Most of the steel industry has managed in general to keep results in the black through the gloomy situation and "in 1997, the bottom line will be stronger," Mer said.
